title: Kolmogorov Arnold networks (KAN) for aerodynamic prediction: a comparison with MLPs and GNNs
authors: Miguel Jaraiz, Fermin Gutierrez, Pablo Yeste, Miguel Sánchez-Domínguez, Eusebio Valero, Gonzalo Rubio
abstract: Kolmogorov Arnold networks (KAN) have recently been introduced as a (deep) neural network architecture whose trainable parameters adapt the activation functions, instead of the coefficients of the affine transformations at the core of traditional architectures such as deep multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). This architecture builds on the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem, which endows it with universal approximation properties. While the advent of KANs has been received with excitement, there is a current debate about the possible KAN supremacy over deep multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) for classic fields such as symbolic regression, generic-purpose machine learning, natural language processing or computer vision. Here we assess the performance of KANs --and its nuanced comparison against MLPs and graph neural networks (GNNs)-- in the realm of fluid dynamics surrogate modelling. To that aim, we consider the task of predicting the surface pressure distribution over subsonic and transonic airfoils, a canonical task in aerodynamics. Our results show that KAN models show good performance in predicting the whole pressure coefficients and is able to interpolate across Mach numbers and angles of attack, however its performance is comparable --marginally inferior-- to a suitably trained MLP, where best performance is achieved by a GNN at the expense or requiring lengthier training. While the optimal KAN model have typically much lower complexity than MLP and GNN --hence resulting in faster training--, we find that KANs suffer from training instabilities, and their performance is highly dependent on a proper hyperparameter optimisation.

infographic.key_insight: KANs can predict airfoil pressure distributions well and interpolate across conditions, but they do not clearly outperform a well-tuned MLP and trail the best GNN in this study.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For aerodynamic surrogate modeling, KANs may offer a lower-complexity and faster-training alternative when accurate pressure prediction is needed across Mach number and angle of attack.
method: Compared KANs against MLPs and graph neural networks for airfoil surface pressure prediction.
Tested subsonic and transonic airfoils with interpolation across Mach numbers and angles of attack.
Evaluated predictive accuracy alongside model complexity and training cost.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper evaluates predicted pressure coefficients for airfoils across subsonic and transonic regimes, finding KAN performance comparable to but slightly below a suitably trained MLP, with the best accuracy from a GNN.
infographic.watch_item: KAN performance is sensitive to hyperparameter tuning and can suffer from training instabilities, so careful optimization is required.
infographic.paper_title: Kolmogorov Arnold networks (KAN) for aerodynamic prediction: a comparison with MLPs and GNNs

title: Kriging and neural network models for pressure losses across perforated plates
authors: Shuai Li
abstract: In this paper, two novel data-driven models based on kriging and neural networks (NN) are proposed to predict pressure losses across perforated plates with circular perforations in turbulent flows. The models are developed using two sets of experimental data available in the literature. The predictive performance of the proposed models is assessed and compared against widely used empirical formulae. It is found that the proposed models consistently outperform existing empirical models for most perforated plate configurations contained in the experimental datasets. Besides, the predicted pressure losses generally show good agreement with experimental measurements, demonstrating that data-driven approaches based on kriging and NN provide a feasible framework for modelling pressure losses across perforated plates. Overall, both approaches are promising, despite being trained on a relatively limited amount of experimental data, owing to the scarcity of measurements reported in the literature. To demonstrate the applicability of the proposed models in numerical simulations, two-dimensional channel flows are simulated using the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations, in which the new pressure-loss models are implemented as a source term in the momentum equations. The RANS predictions are found to be in excellent agreement with the model predictions, confirming the suitability of the proposed approaches for practical computational fluid dynamics applications.

infographic.key_insight: Kriging and neural-network models can predict pressure losses across perforated plates more accurately than standard empirical formulas in turbulent flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The proposed data-driven pressure-loss models can be embedded into RANS simulations to improve CFD predictions for perforated-plate devices.
method: Trained kriging and neural network regressors on two experimental datasets from the literature.
Compared predictions against commonly used empirical pressure-loss correlations.
Implemented the new models as momentum source terms in 2D channel-flow RANS simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the available experimental configurations, both models generally matched measurements well and outperformed existing empirical formulas in most cases.
infographic.watch_item: The models were developed from relatively limited experimental data, so reliability may depend on how well new cases match the training configurations.
infographic.paper_title: Kriging and neural network models for pressure losses across perforated plates

title: Mean-Flow Adjoint Sensitivity Analysis of Unsteady Flow Around Porous Cylinders Using a Homogenized Lattice Boltzmann Method
authors: Shota Ito, Johannes L. Grafen, Fedor Bukreev, Adrian Kummerländer, Mathias J. Krause
abstract: Adjoint-based sensitivity analysis is an indispensable tool for large-scale fluid-dynamic design and distributed control problems, yet its application to unsteady and turbulent flows is frequently hindered by the prohibitive memory footprint of transient checkpointing and the divergence of gradients in chaotic regimes. To address these computational bottlenecks, this paper presents a mean-flow adjoint sensitivity analysis framework for unsteady flows around porous cylinders using the homogenized lattice Boltzmann method (HLBM). Within this framework, solid structures are efficiently modeled as local porous media utilizing a Brinkman penalization approach. We systematically investigate HLBM-based adjoint gradients for drag and energy dissipation objective functionals, transitioning from steady laminar to unsteady, and finally to turbulent flow regimes. For the turbulent case at Re = 3900, a proof-of-concept is conducted where the framework relies on automatic differentiation to automatically generate adjoint kernels containing subgrid-scale (SGS) turbulence models for large eddy simulations (LES), circumventing manual derivation and allowing for a direct comparison against the frozen turbulence assumption (FTA).

infographic.key_insight: A mean-flow adjoint framework with homogenized lattice Boltzmann modeling enables practical sensitivity analysis for unsteady porous-cylinder flows while avoiding costly transient checkpointing and chaotic gradient divergence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a scalable path for optimizing porous flow devices and controlling drag or dissipation in steady, unsteady, and turbulent regimes.
method: Use HLBM with Brinkman penalization to represent porous cylinder geometry as local porous media.
Compute mean-flow adjoint sensitivities for drag and energy-dissipation objectives across flow regimes.
For LES at Re = 3900, generate adjoint kernels automatically with automatic differentiation and compare SGS-aware gradients to frozen turbulence assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a systematic study from steady laminar to unsteady and turbulent flow, including a proof-of-concept LES case at Re = 3900.
infographic.watch_item: Mean-flow and frozen-turbulence approximations may miss fully time-resolved gradient dynamics, so validation is needed before design use in strongly chaotic flows.
infographic.paper_title: Mean-Flow Adjoint Sensitivity Analysis of Unsteady Flow Around Porous Cylinders Using a Homogenized Lattice Boltzmann Method

title: Engineering Collective Microbial Dynamics for Sustainable Thermal Management
authors: Nilanjan Mondal, Soumitree Mishra, Anupam Sengupta
abstract: The rapid growth of energy-intensive technologies, including artificial intelligence, large-scale computing, and thermal management systems, has intensified global energy demand amid accelerating climate change. Meeting these demands requires innovative, low-carbon thermal management strategies that improve energy efficiency while minimizing environmental impact. This review revisits the underexplored phenomenon of bioconvection, a self-organized fluid motion generated by motile microorganisms, as a bio-inspired approach to sustainable heat transfer. Drawing on studies from natural ecosystems and laboratory experiments, we synthesize current knowledge of microorganism-induced hydrodynamics, pattern formation, and thermofluidic transport to assess the feasibility of harnessing bioconvection for thermal management. We further support this assessment through quantitative analyses of the thermal performance of bioconvective systems and discuss this in the framework of relevant non-dimensional numbers. By generating spontaneous convective plumes through density stratification, motile microorganisms enhance heat and mass transfer without external mechanical forcing. These self-organized flows provide a promising route toward hybrid bio-engineered cooling systems that reduce pumping energy, disrupt thermal boundary layers, and improve heat transfer efficiency. We conclude the review with the key challenges on the way to practical implementation, including microbial stability, material compatibility, controllability, scalability, as well as integration with existing cooling technologies. Finally, we identify critical research directions spanning heat transfer, microbiology, and nonlinear fluid mechanics within the broad context of sustainability, positioning bioconvection as a promising strategy for environmentally responsible thermal management in an era of rapidly increasing energy demand.

infographic.key_insight: Motile microorganisms can self-organize into bioconvective flows that passively enhance heat transfer, offering a bio-inspired route to lower-energy thermal management.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Bioconvection could help reduce pumping power, weaken thermal boundary layers, and improve cooling performance in hybrid systems for data centers and other high-heat technologies.
method: Reviewed natural and laboratory studies of microorganism-induced flow and pattern formation.
Synthesized thermofluidic transport mechanisms and relevant non-dimensional numbers.
Assessed thermal performance to judge feasibility for practical cooling applications.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper supports its claims with quantitative analyses of bioconvective thermal performance and interpretation through dimensionless flow and heat-transfer metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Practical deployment is constrained by microbial stability, material compatibility, controllability, scalability, and integration with existing cooling hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Engineering Collective Microbial Dynamics for Sustainable Thermal Management

title: Influence of wind shear and veer on power, thrust, and induction of an actuator disk
authors: Kirby S. Heck, Storm A. Mata, Michael F. Howland
abstract: Wind shear and wind veer (gradients of wind speed and direction, respectively) are ubiquitous in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), and wind turbines therefore routinely operate in sheared and veered conditions. Previous field campaigns have observed statistically significant variations in power production efficiency (quantified by a power coefficient) upwards of 15% due to shear and veer. However, it is not yet clear how non-uniform inflow conditions alter rotor aerodynamics and drive these efficiency variations. In this study, we perform concurrent-precursor large-eddy simulations (LES) of an actuator disk-modeled wind turbine across stratified ABL conditions to demonstrate that shear and veer can reduce wind power efficiency by more than 20%. To support these ABL simulations, we perform simplified inflow LES where shear and veer are controlled independently. Using these controlled simulations, we demonstrate that shear and veer effects can be decomposed into: (1) geometric effects, due to changes in rotor-equivalent wind speed, and (2) inductive effects, which change the rotor aerodynamics and induced velocities. Inductive effects of wind shear modulate the power coefficient through changes to the local induction, while inductive effects of wind veer reduce the power coefficient by generating an adverse pressure gradient at the rotor scale. The geometric and inductive effects of shear and veer approximately linearly superimpose, with increasing losses as shear and veer magnitudes increase. Inductive effects account for a significant fraction of the observed losses, and the induction of a turbine is affected by shear, veer, and wall proximity through processes that are neglected in existing engineering models. Revealing the mechanisms through which shear and veer affect rotor performance establishes a framework that can enable improved power prediction in realistic ABL conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Wind shear and veer can cut actuator-disk power efficiency by more than 20% because their effects are not only geometric but also change induction and rotor aerodynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Turbine power prediction models should account for shear, veer, and wall proximity because inductive losses can be a major part of real ABL performance degradation.
method: Concurrent-precursor LES of an actuator-disk wind turbine in stratified atmospheric boundary layer conditions
Controlled inflow LES with shear and veer varied independently
Decomposition of losses into geometric rotor-equivalent wind-speed effects and inductive aerodynamic effects
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that simulated shear and veer conditions reduced power coefficient by more than 20%, with inductive effects explaining a significant fraction of the loss.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions come from actuator-disk LES and simplified inflow cases, so translating them directly to full-blade turbines and complex terrain may require additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Influence of wind shear and veer on power, thrust, and induction of an actuator disk

title: Gappy Reconstruction of Bubbly Flows by Guided Diffusion Models
authors: Hridey Narula, Tianyi Li, Michele Buzzicotti, Luca Biferale, Prasad Perlekar
abstract: Experiments in multiphase flows are often limited in their ability to simultaneously obtain velocity measurements in different phases. At the same time, flow reconstruction from phase-limited measurements is a challenging problem due to the substantially different velocity statistics across the phases. We address this problem for buoyancy-driven bubbly flows in the pseudo-turbulence regime by using a guided diffusion model. We train the model using two-dimensional slices of the velocity field extracted from fully resolved three-dimensional direct numerical simulations. The model generates physically realistic velocity fields both unconditionally and when conditioned on the surrounding liquid flow. The reconstructed bubble-phase velocity field accurately reproduces key statistical features of the flow. We further show that a simple patching procedure for adjacent two-dimensional slices enables a reasonable reconstruction of the three-dimensional flow inside a bubble. These results establish the potential of diffusion models to serve as generative priors for three-dimensional turbulent multiphase flows, opening a route toward the reconstruction of unobserved or experimentally inaccessible velocity fields from sparse, partial, or phase-limited measurements.

infographic.key_insight: A guided diffusion model can reconstruct phase-limited bubbly-flow velocity fields, including the difficult bubble phase, from sparse 2D slices while preserving key flow statistics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical route to recover unmeasured or experimentally inaccessible velocities in multiphase turbulence, improving diagnosis and modeling of bubbly flow experiments.
method: Train a diffusion model on 2D velocity slices extracted from fully resolved 3D DNS of buoyancy-driven bubbly flows.
Condition generation on surrounding liquid-flow information to reconstruct missing phase-limited fields.
Use a simple patching scheme across adjacent slices to extend reconstruction toward 3D bubble interiors.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the generated fields are physically realistic and that the bubble-phase reconstructions accurately reproduce key statistical features, with reasonable 3D reconstruction from adjacent slices.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is demonstrated on DNS-derived slices in a specific pseudo-turbulent regime, so transfer to real experimental data and more complex multiphase settings may require careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Gappy Reconstruction of Bubbly Flows by Guided Diffusion Models

title: GQL-Based Physical-Constraint-Preserving High-Order Finite Difference Schemes for Special Relativistic Hydrodynamics in Arbitrary Dimensions
authors: Linfeng Xu, Shengrong Ding, Kailiang Wu
abstract: High-order accurate simulations of special relativistic hydrodynamics (RHD) are prone to numerical breakdown if intrinsic physical constraints (positive rest-mass density/pressure and subluminal velocity) are violated near strong discontinuities. In this work, we develop a robust and efficient physical-constraint-preserving (PCP) flux-limiting framework for high-order schemes, using finite-difference WENO as a representative example. By leveraging the geometric quasilinearization (GQL) representation, which equivalently reformulates the nonlinear RHD constraints into a family of linear inequalities, we integrate a Zalesak-type Flux-Corrected Transport (FCT) update into a scalar-style limiter that acts directly on conservative variables. A critical innovation is the explicit, non-iterative determination of limiting parameters via a rational stereographic parameterization of the GQL normal vector. This technique transforms the required worst-case minimization over auxiliary variables into a generalized Rayleigh-quotient formulation, allowing the optimal parameters to be obtained by solving small symmetric eigenvalue problems ($2\times2$ in 1D; $(d+1)\times(d+1)$ in $d$ dimensions). Relaxed variants are further introduced to reduce computational costs in multidimensions while retaining the PCP guarantee. Extensive numerical benchmarks ranging from 1D to 3D, including ultra-relativistic Riemann problems and astrophysical jets, demonstrate that the proposed method robustly enforces physical admissibility, sharply resolves discontinuities, and maintains design-order accuracy for smooth solutions.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns special relativistic hydrodynamics into a physically admissible high-order solver by enforcing positivity and subluminal constraints through a GQL-based flux limiter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables robust, accurate CFD simulations of shocks, jets, and other extreme relativistic flows without numerical breakdown near strong discontinuities.
method: Reformulate RHD admissibility conditions into linear inequalities using geometric quasilinearization (GQL).
Embed a Zalesak-type flux-corrected transport limiter directly on conservative variables in a finite-difference WENO framework.
Compute optimal limiting parameters non-iteratively via stereographic parameterization and small symmetric eigenvalue problems.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method is validated on extensive 1D–3D benchmarks, including ultra-relativistic Riemann problems and astrophysical jets, showing preserved physical constraints and design-order accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: The limiter adds extra eigenvalue-based per-cell cost, and the relaxed multidimensional variants trade some exactness for efficiency.
infographic.paper_title: GQL-Based Physical-Constraint-Preserving High-Order Finite Difference Schemes for Special Relativistic Hydrodynamics in Arbitrary Dimensions

title: Data-driven linear analysis of turbulent flows
authors: Benjamin Herrmann, Katherine Cao, Carlos A. Gonzalez, S. L. Brunton, Beverley J. McKeon
abstract: Mean-flow-based linear analyses of turbulent flows, such as resolvent analysis, provide valuable insight about flow structures and their dynamics that has been widely leveraged to model, control and understand the underlying flow physics. However, these analyses are computationally expensive for flows over complex geometries and require the use of specialized codes that are typically only available in research environments. On the other hand, data-driven modal decompositions, such as the dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), identify turbulent flow structures that, although statistically relevant, do not provide insight into the physical mechanisms driving their dynamics. Here we introduce a novel data-driven method -- nonlinearity-subtracted DMD (NSDMD) -- that leverages knowledge of the structure of the Navier--Stokes equations to ensure that the learned operator is a low-rank approximation of the underlying mean-flow-linearized dynamics. Specifically, the method uses snapshots of the nonlinear terms in the perturbation equations to explicitly account for the contribution of the nonlinear forcing to the dynamics. We demonstrate the use of NSDMD to perform data-driven resolvent analysis on direct numerical simulation (DNS) and large-eddy simulation (LES) datasets, starting with a minimal channel flow and scaling up to the flow over a full aircraft model. As a result, NSDMD allows performing linear analyses of turbulent flows as a post-processing step on simulation data obtained with any available high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) code.

infographic.key_insight: Nonlinearity-subtracted DMD (NSDMD) uses nonlinear-term snapshots to recover a low-rank, mean-flow-linearized operator from data, enabling resolvent-style analysis without specialized linear-solver infrastructure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes linear modal analysis of turbulent flows practical as a post-processing step on DNS/LES data, even for complex geometries such as a full aircraft model.
method: Compute DMD while subtracting the explicit contribution of nonlinear forcing in the perturbation equations.
Use the resulting operator as a data-driven approximation of mean-flow-linearized dynamics.
Apply the framework to data-driven resolvent analysis across simple and complex turbulent flows.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstrations on DNS and LES datasets, progressing from a minimal channel flow to a full aircraft model.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality and availability of nonlinear-term snapshots, and the learned operator is still an approximation of the underlying linearized physics.
infographic.paper_title: Data-driven linear analysis of turbulent flows

title: New numerical methods for calculating statistical equilibria of two-dimensional turbulent flows, strictly based on the Miller-Robert-Sommeria theory
authors: Koki Ryono, Keiichi Ishioka
abstract: New numerical methods are proposed for the mixing entropy maximization problem in the context of Miller-Robert-Sommeria's (MRS) statistical mechanics theory of two-dimensional turbulence, particularly in the case of spherical geometry. Two of the methods are for the canonical problem; the other is for the microcanonical problem. The methods are based on the original MRS theory and thus take into account all Casimir invariants. Compared to the methods proposed in previous studies, our new methods make it easier to detect multiple statistical equilibria and to search for solutions with broken zonal symmetry. The methods are applied to a zonally symmetric initial vorticity distribution which is barotropically unstable. Two statistical equilibria are obtained, one of which has a wave-like structure with zonal wavenumber 1, and the other has a wave-like structure with zonal wavenumber 2. While the former is the maximum point of the mixing entropy, the wavenumber 2 structure of the latter is nearly the same as the structure that appears in the end state of the time integration of the vorticity equation. The new methods allow for efficient computation of statistical equilibria for initial vorticity distributions consisting of many levels of vorticity patches without losing information about all the conserved quantities. This means that the statistical equilibria can be obtained from an arbitrary initial vorticity distribution, which allows for the application of statistical mechanics to interpret a wide variety of flow patterns appearing in geophysical fluids.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces MRS-theory-based numerical methods that can efficiently find multiple statistical equilibria of two-dimensional turbulent flows, including symmetry-broken states on a sphere.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These methods improve practical prediction and interpretation of geophysical flow patterns by preserving all Casimir invariants and handling arbitrary initial vorticity distributions.
method: Canonical and microcanonical entropy-maximization solvers derived directly from Miller-Robert-Sommeria theory
Designed to detect multiple equilibria and search beyond zonal symmetry
Applied to a barotropically unstable zonal vorticity field on spherical geometry
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors report two equilibria from the test case: a zonal wavenumber-1 maximum-entropy state and a wavenumber-2 state that closely matches the time-integrated vorticity equation outcome.
infographic.watch_item: The approach may be computationally demanding for high-dimensional vorticity distributions and still requires careful handling of convergence when multiple equilibria coexist.
infographic.paper_title: New numerical methods for calculating statistical equilibria of two-dimensional turbulent flows, strictly based on the Miller-Robert-Sommeria theory

title: Electrophoretic motion of a liquid droplet with Brinkman-screened internal hydrodynamics
authors: Sutapa Mandal, Subrata Majhi
abstract: We develop a theory for the electrophoresis of a spherical porous liquid droplet with prescribed uniform surface charge. The exterior electrokinetics is governed by the Poisson-Nernst-Planck-Stokes equations, while the internal liquid motion is described by the Brinkman-Debye-Bueche equation. A regular perturbation expansion in the applied electric field reduces the governing equations to coupled radial ordinary differential equations. In the Debye-Hückel regime, we derive a closed-form mobility expression valid for arbitrary Debye layer thickness. The analysis shows that the porous interior modifies clean-droplet electrophoresis through a single Brinkman-screened hydrodynamic resistance, yielding a continuous transition between clean-droplet and rigid-particle limits. Numerical solutions beyond the low-potential regime reveal a non-universal role of permeability: increasing the Darcy number can either suppress or enhance the mobility. This reversal is determined by the sign of the interfacial-velocity mode, which is governed by the competition between tangential Maxwell traction and hydrodynamic shear generated by electric-double-layer distortion. Dielectric polarization, surface charge and double-layer thickness can reverse the internal circulation, while the Darcy number controls how strongly this circulation is transmitted through the porous interior. This permeability sensitivity is especially pronounced for highly polarizable droplets in the thin-double-layer regime. The theory provides a basis for tuning electrokinetic transport of soft porous droplets in microfluidic and biomedical technologies.

infographic.key_insight: A porous liquid droplet’s electrophoretic mobility is controlled by a single Brinkman-screened hydrodynamic resistance, creating a smooth bridge between clean-droplet and rigid-particle behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a tunable design rule for microfluidic and biomedical transport of soft charged droplets, where permeability, surface charge, and double-layer thickness can be adjusted to control motion.
method: Coupled Poisson-Nernst-Planck-Stokes equations outside the droplet with Brinkman-Debye-Bueche hydrodynamics inside.
Used a regular perturbation expansion in electric-field strength to reduce the problem to radial ODEs.
Derived a closed-form Debye-Hückel mobility expression and validated behavior beyond low potential with numerical solutions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical derivations plus numerical solutions over arbitrary Debye-layer thickness and beyond the low-potential regime, showing mobility can either increase or decrease with Darcy number.
infographic.watch_item: Permeability effects are non-universal: mobility trends can reverse depending on interfacial-velocity mode, dielectric polarization, and double-layer conditions, so design predictions require case-specific evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Electrophoretic motion of a liquid droplet with Brinkman-screened internal hydrodynamics

title: Offline accuracy is not enough: closed-loop instability and stabilisation of a wall-sensor neural estimator in opposition control
authors: Giorgio Maria Cavallazzi, Miguel Pérez-Cuadrado, Alfredo Pinelli
abstract: Opposition control reduces skin-friction drag by opposing the wall-normal velocity on a near-wall detection plane, but the detection-plane velocity it requires is not available from wall-mounted sensors. Wall data can reconstruct inner-flow quantities accurately when assessed offline on a fixed flow state, and we ask whether such a reconstructed field can instead serve as a live surrogate sensor inside the feedback loop. We train a recurrent estimator to infer the detection-plane velocity from the two wall-shear-stress components in opposition-controlled turbulence. Offline it performs extremely well, reaching a correlation of 0.99 and near-unity coherence across the energetic scales; yet the same estimator fails in closed loop, decorrelating from the true field within a few viscous time units as the control collapses. The failure is not one of accuracy but of distribution shift induced by the controller itself: small closed-loop errors carry the flow off the attractor represented in the training data, while unresolved high-wavenumber errors enter through the wall boundary condition and return as out-of-distribution inputs. Standard remedies such as low-pass filtering and exponential averaging only delay numerical breakdown while accelerating decorrelation. Stable wall-only control is recovered by imposing spectral consistency on the deployed actuation and retraining the estimator on its own closed-loop data, giving a controller that holds much of the drag reduction of ideal opposition control from wall quantities alone. The obstacle is not whether the near-wall flow can be reconstructed offline, but whether that reconstruction stays dynamically consistent when allowed to modify the flow it senses.

infographic.key_insight: A wall-sensor neural estimator can be highly accurate offline yet still destabilize opposition control in closed loop because the controller changes the data distribution the model sees.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For drag-reduction systems, deployment must be judged by closed-loop stability and sensor-actuator consistency, not just by offline reconstruction accuracy.
method: Train a recurrent estimator to predict near-wall detection-plane velocity from the two wall-shear-stress components.
Embed the estimator inside opposition control and test whether offline accuracy transfers to live feedback.
Stabilize deployment using spectral consistency in the actuation and retraining on closed-loop data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The estimator reaches about 0.99 correlation and near-unity coherence offline, but in closed loop it decorrelates within a few viscous time units as drag reduction collapses.
infographic.watch_item: Low-pass filtering and exponential averaging can postpone numerical failure but may accelerate loss of correlation; closed-loop retraining is needed for robust deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Offline accuracy is not enough: closed-loop instability and stabilisation of a wall-sensor neural estimator in opposition control

title: Premixed flames in a stagnation point flow under Darcy's law
authors: Prabakaran Rajamanickam, Joel Daou
abstract: Premixed flames in stagnation point flows are traditionally described using Navier--Stokes equations where inertia and density variations play an important part in determining the flame structure. However, in porous media or Hele-Shaw configurations, Darcy's law replaces the momentum balance, shifting the governing physics to a balance between pressure and viscous forces. This study investigates non-adiabatic strained premixed flames under Darcy's law, pertinent in particular to confined flames in Hele-Shaw burners, accounting for non-unity Lewis numbers and volumetric heat losses. The flame is established in a planar counterflow formed by impinging a cold unburnt gas and a hot burnt gas maintained at the adiabatic flame temperature. We show that the jump in the strain rate across the flame is associated with a jump in viscosity, rather than, as in the classical Navier--Stokes case, a jump in density. Furthermore, the ratio of viscosity to the density-permeability product $μ/ρκ$, i.e., kinematic viscous resistance, is identified as a key coordinate stretching factor in the mathematical description of the flame structure. This ratio increases significantly across the flame. As a result: (1) the burnt gas acts as a strong viscous barrier, (2) for an increasing strain rate, flame migration towards the burnt gas is hindered, (3) for a decreasing strain rate, migration towards the unburnt gas is promoted, and (4) streamline refraction is augmented. By analysing the burning rate across varying strain rates and heat-loss parameters, we identify distinct extinction and ignition regimes that fundamentally differ from classical combustion theory, thereby providing new insights into flame stabilisation in friction-dominated environments and under confinement.

infographic.key_insight: In Darcy-flow stagnation-point flames, the dominant flame-structure jump is driven by a viscosity change across the flame, making the burnt gas a viscous barrier that strongly alters strain, migration, and extinction behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for confined premixed combustion in porous media and Hele-Shaw burners, where friction-dominated flow can change flame stabilization, heat-loss sensitivity, and operating limits.
method: Model premixed counterflow flames under Darcy’s law instead of Navier–Stokes
Include non-unity Lewis number effects and volumetric heat losses
Analyze strain-rate variation, flame migration, streamline refraction, and burning-rate-based ignition/extinction regimes
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports parametric analysis of burning rate versus strain rate and heat-loss parameters, revealing distinct extinction and ignition regimes.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are specific to Darcy-flow, confined configurations with simplified momentum physics, so direct transfer to inertia-dominated or unconfined flames may be limited.
infographic.paper_title: Premixed flames in a stagnation point flow under Darcy's law

title: Lagrangian velocity statistics of homogeneous isotropic turbulence in dilute polymer solutions
authors: Yusuke Koide, Susumu Goto
abstract: We conduct direct numerical simulations of homogeneous isotropic turbulence in dilute polymer solutions to investigate the Lagrangian velocity statistics. We show how polymers modulate the power spectral density of the Lagrangian velocity and the Lagrangian integral timescale by varying the Reynolds number, forcing method, and polymer relaxation time. As the polymer relaxation time increases, the attenuation of the power spectral density extends successively from high to low frequencies, and the Lagrangian integral timescale increases. To clarify the mechanism underlying the modulation of the Lagrangian velocity statistics, we decompose the Lagrangian velocity into the contributions from vortices at different length scales. Using this scale-decomposition analysis, we demonstrate that the observed modulation of the Lagrangian velocity statistics results from polymer-induced suppression of vortices that proceeds from smaller to larger scales.

infographic.key_insight: In dilute polymer solutions, increasing polymer relaxation time shifts Lagrangian velocity attenuation from high to low frequencies and lengthens the Lagrangian integral timescale because polymers suppress vortical motion from small to large scales.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This helps predict and control turbulence transport and mixing in polymer processing, drag-reduction flows, and other viscoelastic fluid systems.
method: Direct numerical simulation of homogeneous isotropic turbulence with dilute polymer solutions
Varied Reynolds number, forcing method, and polymer relaxation time
Performed scale-decomposition of Lagrangian velocity to isolate contributions from vortices at different length scales
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports changes in the Lagrangian power spectral density and integral timescale across simulated conditions, linking these trends to scale-dependent vortex suppression.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions come from DNS of homogeneous isotropic turbulence, so transfer to wall-bounded or strongly inhomogeneous industrial flows may require additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Lagrangian velocity statistics of homogeneous isotropic turbulence in dilute polymer solutions

title: Exact analytical solutions for the piston effect in supercritical fluids under post-acoustic approximation -- Short-time asymptotics, thermal penetration depth and comparison with the Spacelab D-2 experiments
authors: Mátyás Szücs
abstract: Near the liquid-vapor critical point, fluids become highly compressible, giving rise to a special, strongly coupled thermo-mechanical process: the piston effect. In this phenomenon, a thin thermal boundary layer develops near a heated wall; owing to strong thermal expansion, this layer acts like a piston, compressing the bulk fluid adiabatically and resulting in a seemingly accelerated thermal response. Although the piston effect is a thermo-acoustic process, the characteristic time scale of the boundary perturbation is typically orders of magnitude larger than the acoustic time scale of the setup. Consequently, rapid acoustic propagation can be neglected, justifying a post-acoustic approximation with a spatially uniform but time-dependent bulk pressure. Within the linear regime, the temporal evolution of pressure can be directly connected to the heat flux entering through the boundaries. As a result, the problem reduces to a diffusion equation governed by a spatially homogeneous source term that depends explicitly on the boundary conditions. Exact, closed-form analytical solutions are derived for effectively one-dimensional problems in both Cartesian and spherical coordinates, considering boundary conditions of the first and second kinds. Short-time asymptotic behavior and thermal penetration depth are analyzed for all four cases. By incorporating the heat capacity of a container via a homogeneous model, an effective boundary condition coupling the wall heat flux and the time derivative of the wall temperature is derived, allowing for a direct comparison with experimental data from the Spacelab D-2 mission. The analytical predictions show good agreement with the experimental results without relying on any numerical simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Under post-acoustic approximation, the piston effect in supercritical fluids reduces to a diffusion problem with a spatially uniform pressure source, enabling exact analytical solutions for the thermal response.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives engineers a fast, closed-form way to predict heat transfer and bulk pressurization in near-critical systems without resolving acoustic waves or running full simulations.
method: Derive exact 1D analytical solutions in Cartesian and spherical geometries.
Treat pressure as spatially uniform and time-dependent, linked directly to boundary heat flux.
Introduce an effective boundary condition that accounts for container heat capacity and wall temperature evolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The analytical model is compared with Spacelab D-2 experiment data and is reported to match well without numerical simulation.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on a linear, post-acoustic approximation, so accuracy may degrade when acoustic dynamics or strong nonlinear effects become important.
infographic.paper_title: Exact analytical solutions for the piston effect in supercritical fluids under post-acoustic approximation -- Short-time asymptotics, thermal penetration depth and comparison with the Spacelab D-2 experiments

title: Monolithic kinetic algorithm for heterogeneous porous media systems using a continuous one-domain approach
authors: Nikita O. Gusev, Ilya V. Karlin
abstract: We propose a lattice Boltzmann model (LBM) on standard lattices for simulating multi-dimensional, weakly compressible, isothermal flows within and around isotropic heterogeneous porous media. The model incorporates Darcy-Forchheimer drag and a Brinkman-like effective viscous stress tensor. In the hydrodynamic limit, it recovers a generalized volume-averaged formulation valid in both free-fluid and porous-medium regions. By relying on a single kinetic equation and a monolithic LBM algorithm, the formulation provides a one-domain solver for free-fluid/porous-medium interactions. Unlike previous LBM formulations for porous media, the proposed model recovers the correct porosity scaling of both the pressure and convective terms, while preserving the isotropy, and hence the Galilean invariance, of the viscous stress tensor. Linear and nonlinear drag, variable-porosity corrections, and additional body forces are incorporated through a consistent generalized forcing scheme. The model allows the speed of sound to be specified independently thereby improving computational efficiency. In addition, it includes a freely tunable effective bulk viscosity that can be used to enhance numerical stability. Model performance was evaluated using 2D benchmark flow problems. The ability of the proposed LBM model to simulate transport between free-fluid and heterogeneous porous regions within a one-domain framework enables a broad range of applications, particularly in early-stage, device-scale design studies of engineered porous structures with spatially varying porosity.

infographic.key_insight: A single monolithic lattice Boltzmann formulation can model both free-fluid and heterogeneous porous regions in one domain while correctly capturing porosity-scaled pressure, convection, and viscous stress.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables efficient simulation of coupled flow through and around porous structures for device-scale design, where porosity varies spatially and fluid–porous interfaces must be handled consistently.
method: Uses a standard-lattice LBM with one kinetic equation for weakly compressible, isothermal flow.
Adds Darcy-Forchheimer drag, Brinkman-like viscous stress, variable-porosity corrections, and generalized forcing in a unified framework.
Allows independent tuning of sound speed and effective bulk viscosity to improve efficiency and stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was evaluated on 2D benchmark flow problems and shown to reproduce free-fluid/porous interactions within a one-domain solver.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy and stability likely depend on careful parameterization of porosity, drag, and forcing terms, especially near sharp fluid–porous transitions.
infographic.paper_title: Monolithic kinetic algorithm for heterogeneous porous media systems using a continuous one-domain approach

title: Flexibility as a Universal Nature-Inspired Mechanism for Thrust Enhancement
authors: Roberta Santoriello, Francesco Viola, Vincenzo Citro
abstract: Nature has equipped jet-propelled swimmers with flexible nozzles that outperform rigid ones, yet the origin of this advantage has remained unexplained. By tracking where and when energy is exchanged between fluid and structure, three-dimensional numerical simulations resolve the underlying mechanism: a standing-wave response of the nozzle, in which the structure dilates and then recoils synchronously, charging and releasing energy to enhance thrust. Outside of this regime, the structure exhibits a traveling wave response, with expansion and contraction coexisting along the nozzle, reducing the thrust gain. We propose a physics-based model that captures the boundary between standing and traveling responses in a closed form, showing that the optimum occurs when the natural period of the structure matches the pulse duration. Beyond this optimum the strain imposed by the nozzle curvature required for steering selects the geometry observed across marine species. The propulsion and maneuverability are reconciled within a single framework that yields design principles for soft robotic propulsors.

infographic.key_insight: Flexible jet nozzles enhance thrust when they respond with a standing-wave motion that synchronizes dilation and recoil with the jet pulse, enabling efficient energy exchange with the fluid.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This identifies a design rule for soft propulsors and steerable nozzles: tune structural flexibility so the natural period matches the forcing duration, balancing thrust gain and maneuverability.
method: 3D numerical simulations track where and when energy is exchanged between fluid and structure
Compare standing-wave and traveling-wave nozzle responses to explain thrust differences
Derive a closed-form physics-based model for the boundary between response regimes
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evidence from three-dimensional numerical simulations and a closed-form model, with the optimum occurring when the structure’s natural period matches the pulse duration.
infographic.watch_item: The optimum thrust benefit depends on matching structural timing to the jet pulse and on curvature/steering constraints, so the design may be sensitive to geometry and operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Flexibility as a Universal Nature-Inspired Mechanism for Thrust Enhancement

title: Effects of thermochemical modelling on a hypersonic shock-wave/turbulent boundary-layer interaction
authors: Marco Fratini, Pedro Stefanin Volpiani, Matteo Bernardini
abstract: Thermochemical non-equilibrium can alter the structure, loads, and time scales of hypersonic shock-wave/turbulent boundary-layer interactions, yet its role in fully turbulent configurations remains largely unquantified. The present work addresses this issue by performing three direct numerical simulations of an oblique shock impinging on a turbulent high-enthalpy boundary layer at edge Mach number $M_e=6.4$ and stagnation enthalpy $H_e=16.9$ MJ/kg. The simulations share identical geometry and freestream conditions, but employ a hierarchy of progressively simplified thermochemical descriptions: a finite-rate reactive case, a single-species thermally perfect gas model, and a single-species calorically perfect model. The reactive simulation shows that the shock-induced temperature rise substantially enhances chemical activity relative to the incoming boundary layer, with peak concentrations of dissociation products attained downstream of the interaction. Thus, the thermal and chemical responses are not synchronised: the composition lags the rapid thermal forcing imposed by the shock system, and turbulent Damköhler numbers reach values of order unity within the recirculation region, indicating non-negligible turbulence-chemistry interaction. The comparison among the three models shows that thermally and calorically perfect descriptions yield similar predictions, whereas finite-rate chemistry produces systematic differences: a smaller separation bubble, lower post-interaction wall heat flux, lower mean and fluctuating temperatures, and a less inclined reflected shock. In the present regime, the dominant modelling distinction is therefore between frozen and chemically reacting descriptions, with caloric-model effects playing only a secondary role.

infographic.key_insight: Finite-rate chemistry significantly changes hypersonic shock/turbulent boundary-layer interaction physics, while thermally vs. calorically perfect gas assumptions make only secondary differences.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For hypersonic vehicle design, using a frozen/chemically reacting model can materially affect predicted separation, wall heating, and shock structure, impacting thermal protection and load estimates.
method: 3 direct numerical simulations of an oblique shock impinging on a turbulent high-enthalpy boundary layer.
Compared finite-rate reactive chemistry against single-species thermally perfect and calorically perfect gas models.
Held geometry and freestream conditions fixed at Me = 6.4 and He = 16.9 MJ/kg to isolate thermochemical-model effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the reactive case yields a smaller separation bubble, lower post-interaction wall heat flux, lower mean/fluctuating temperatures, and a less inclined reflected shock than the simplified gas models.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are specific to this Mach/enthalpy regime and the chosen DNS setup, so extrapolation to other hypersonic conditions or wall/catalysis effects should be done cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: Effects of thermochemical modelling on a hypersonic shock-wave/turbulent boundary-layer interaction

title: Dripping-onto-droplet rheometry of sodium alginate solutions
authors: Nada Nazzal, Martin Drahé, Ricardo El Khoury, Irineu Lopes Palhares Junior, Cassio Oishi, Roney Leon Thompson
abstract: In this experimental and theoretical study, we assess the extensional relaxation time of sodium alginate solutions by using dripping-onto-droplet capillary breakup rheometry (DoD), e.g., the capillary thinning and breakup of viscoelastic filaments formed following the coalescence of a millimetric-nozzle-generated pendant drop with a lower droplet cap of the same fluid contained in a millimetric pool in ambient air. Hence, we extend the analyses conducted by El Khoury et al. (2026) from Newtonian to viscoelastic fluids. Our approach relies on experiments recorded with a high-speed camera using sodium alginate in deionised water, with alginate concentrations ranging from 0.1% to 8% by weight. The results are depicted by considering the dynamics of fluid filament thinning, stress balances, and scaling laws. Extensional relaxation times are resolved from the filament diameter evolution. Three flow regimes are highlighted: capillary-inertial, capillary-elastic, and mixed capillary-inertio-elastic. The findings are summarised in a two-dimensional diagram that correlates the filament breakup time with different flow regimes using the important dimensionless parameter of the problem, e.g., the intrinsic Deborah number (which relates the extensional relaxation time to the characteristic capillary-inertial time). This diagram can be used to quantify both the solution's extensional relaxation time and the liquid/air surface tension solely from filament breakup times.

infographic.key_insight: Dripping-onto-droplet breakup can be used as a simple capillary-thinning test to extract the extensional relaxation time of sodium alginate solutions across multiple flow regimes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical way to estimate viscoelastic relaxation and surface tension from breakup timing alone, useful for screening and tuning polymer solutions in fluid processing and formulation.
method: High-speed imaging of a pendant drop coalescing with a lower droplet in air
Analyze filament diameter evolution using stress balances and scaling laws
Classify breakup into capillary-inertial, capillary-elastic, and mixed regimes
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on sodium alginate in deionised water at 0.1% to 8% by weight were used to resolve relaxation times from filament thinning and to build a breakup-time diagram tied to the intrinsic Deborah number.
infographic.watch_item: The regime map and extracted parameters depend on accurate high-speed imaging and careful interpretation of mixed capillary-inertio-elastic breakup behavior.
infographic.paper_title: Dripping-onto-droplet rheometry of sodium alginate solutions

title: Sudden expansion stability thresholds modified by lateral flows
authors: T. Salamon, R. Debuysschère, A. Chafaï, B. Scheid, F. Gallaire
abstract: We study the flow in a symmetric three-dimensional confined sudden expansion with lateral inflow at Reynolds number below 300 and varying lateral-to-central flow rate ratio, using experiments, linear stability analysis, weakly nonlinear theory, and direct numerical simulations. Three distinct flow regimes are identified. Outside an intermediate band of lateral-to-central flow rate ratio, the flow undergoes a steady symmetry-breaking bifurcation above a critical Reynolds number, deflecting the central jet toward one side wall; weakly nonlinear analysis shows this bifurcation to be supercritical, excepting a very narrow parametric range. Within the intermediate band, no such critical Reynolds number exists and direct numerical simulations confirm that residual velocity asymmetries reflect the imposed geometric imperfections rather than intrinsic amplification. Fluctuations observed experimentally in the intermediate band of lateral-to-central flow rate ratio remain unexplained and warrant further investigation.

infographic.key_insight: Lateral inflow can suppress the usual symmetry-breaking instability in a confined sudden expansion, creating an intermediate flow-rate band with no critical Reynolds number for jet deflection.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Designers of microfluidic and internal-flow devices should account for side inflow because it can shift or eliminate stability thresholds and alter jet attachment behavior.
method: Experiments in a symmetric 3D confined sudden expansion
Linear stability analysis and weakly nonlinear theory
Direct numerical simulations across varying lateral-to-central flow-rate ratios
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports three distinct regimes, a supercritical symmetry-breaking bifurcation outside the intermediate band, and DNS confirmation that residual asymmetries in the intermediate band are due to geometric imperfections rather than intrinsic growth.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental fluctuations in the intermediate lateral-flow band remain unexplained, so the mechanism there is not yet fully resolved.
infographic.paper_title: Sudden expansion stability thresholds modified by lateral flows

title: Hydrodynamic theory of premixed flames under Darcy's law: Interfacial conditions and effects of nonunity Lewis number and heat loss
authors: Prabakaran Rajamanickam, Joel Daou
abstract: Premixed flames propagating in porous media or Hele-Shaw channels are governed by Darcy's law, which accounts for the strong frictional forces imposed by the solid matrix or confining walls. Prior theoretical studies of such flames have typically employed phenomenological Markstein-type corrections and have assumed unity Lewis numbers and adiabatic conditions. In this work, we develop a rigorous hydrodynamic theory for premixed flames under Darcy's law that incorporates nonunity Lewis numbers and heat losses. Using large activation-energy asymptotics and a systematic multiple-scale analysis, we derive the interfacial jump conditions across the flame from first principles. The conventional continuity requirements of mass flux and pressure at an interface under Darcy's law acquire corrections to the finite thickness of the flame. The adiabatic burning rate is shown to involve three distinct Markstein numbers, corresponding to curvature, tangential flow strain, and gravity-induced strain. The gravity term is unique to Darcy's law and has no counterpart in classical Navier--Stokes formulations. Moreover, the curvature Markstein number and the tangential strain Markstein number are found to be unequal, in contrast to the classical case where they coincide under constant transport properties. Explicit formulas for the Markstein numbers are provided, and the resulting new dispersion relation, linking the perturbation wave number $k$ to the growth rate $s$, takes the form $s = (a|k| - bk^2 - d|k|^3) / (1 + c|k|)$. This relation, applicable under Darcy's law, is to be compared to the classical Clavin--Garcia dispersion relation derived from the Navier--Stokes equations. The theory provides a rigorous foundation for flame dynamics in strongly confined environments, with direct applications to porous media combustion and Hele-Shaw cell experiments.

infographic.key_insight: A first-principles hydrodynamic theory for premixed flames in Darcy-flow media shows that finite flame thickness, nonunity Lewis number, and heat loss modify interface conditions and introduce distinct curvature, tangential-strain, and gravity-driven Markstein effects.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide a more accurate stability and dispersion model for flames in porous media and Hele-Shaw channels, improving prediction of flame wrinkling, propagation, and confinement-driven instabilities.
method: Used large activation-energy asymptotics to derive flame-interface jump conditions from the governing equations.
Applied a systematic multiple-scale analysis under Darcy's law with nonunity Lewis number and heat loss.
Derived a new dispersion relation: s = (a|k| - bk^2 - d|k|^3)/(1 + c|k|), and explicit Markstein numbers.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an analytical derivation from theory rather than new experimental or simulation data, culminating in explicit interfacial conditions and a closed-form dispersion relation.
infographic.watch_item: The formulation is asymptotic and assumes a Darcy-flow, strongly confined regime, so accuracy may degrade outside thin-flame, large-activation-energy, or porous/Hele-Shaw conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Hydrodynamic theory of premixed flames under Darcy's law: Interfacial conditions and effects of nonunity Lewis number and heat loss
